title: The Broken Prom
premise: Tamsin Thornbury, the only out kid in the dying mill town of Harrow Bend, discovers that the school's legendary ghost is actually the memory of Wren Calloway, a student erased from every record in 1998 after she threatened to expose the school board's cover-up of a fatal hazing. The ghost's impossible-ink notes are fragments of Wren's suppressed testimony, and they choose Tamsin because he, like her, refuses to disappear quietly. As graduation and the final spring audition approach, Tamsin must reconstruct what was buried, confront the board members who are now the town's most respected citizens, and decide whether justice means exposure or something stranger. In the end, he stages the truth as a performance at the audition itself, forcing the town to remember Wren, and the ghost — finally witnessed — lets go.
about_author: Ada Yarrow grew up in a small river town where the high school burned down twice and nobody ever said why, an experience that taught her how communities curate their own pasts. She writes young adult fiction about queer kids who refuse to be footnotes, and lives somewhere with better libraries than her hometown ever managed.

chapters.title: Nine Hundred People, One of Me
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He maps his senior year like a prison sentence: the cafeteria gauntlet, the spring musical audition notice, his one friend Dee. Establishes Harrow Bend's suffocating intimacy and his survival strategy of invisibility. Emotional beat: weary, wry loneliness that masks real fear.

chapters.title: The Note in the Mirror Room
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Cleaning duty in the old auditorium, he finds a note tucked behind a mirror: 'They made me a rumor. Don't let them make you one.' The ink is rust-brown and warm to the touch, though the paper is decades old. Beat: first crack in his numbness — someone sees him.

chapters.title: What Everyone Knows About the Ghost
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Dee recounts the school legend: a girl who died backstage in '98, whose name no one can recall. Tamsin realizes the legend has been sanded smooth on purpose. Beat: the thrill of shared conspiracy, tempered by Dee's warning that some questions get kids hurt.

chapters.title: Yearbooks With a Hole In Them
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Library archives show a torn spine in every 1998 yearbook and a gap in the photo wall. The librarian, Mrs. Okonkwo, catches him — then quietly slips him a key to the basement stacks. Beat: the vertigo of discovering deliberate erasure.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In the basement he finds a single surviving program with a name inked out but legible under raking light: Wren Calloway. That night, a new note appears in his locker, addressed 'Dear Tamsin' — his name, spelled right, in impossible ink. Beat: terror braided with purpose.

chapters.title: The Board of Distinguished Men
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Research reveals four of the five current school board members were seniors in 1998, including beloved coach-turned-superintendent Dale Pruitt. A fifth classmate, Marcus Vey, left town abruptly and never came back. Beat: dread as the ghost story acquires living villains.

chapters.title: Notes From a Locked Room
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The notes escalate — pages of Wren's testimony appearing in places only Tamsin would look, describing a hazing ritual gone wrong and a cover-up voted on over pizza. The ink burns faintly when he lies to himself about wanting to quit. Beat: compulsion; he can't stop reading.

chapters.title: Pruitt Shakes My Hand
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Superintendent Pruitt publicly praises Tamsin at assembly — a calculated kindness that reads as a warning. Afterwards Pruitt mentions the auditorium is scheduled for demolition after graduation. Beat: the mask of benevolent power, and Tamsin's first taste of being watched.

chapters.title: Audition Sides
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Auditions for the final spring musical begin; Tamsin, dragged in by Dee, stuns everyone by singing — his first public act of visibility. Pruitt watches from the back. Beat: exhilaration curdling into awareness that visibility is exactly what got Wren destroyed.

chapters.title: Marcus Vey Answers the Phone
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tracking Vey to a trailer park two states away, Tamsin calls him. Vey, drunk and terrified, confirms the hazing death and says the notes are impossible — 'because I watched them burn everything she wrote.' Then he hangs up. Beat: confirmation and despair; the evidence shouldn't exist.

chapters.title: What Ink Remembers
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin tests the notes against the library's microfilm: every fact checks out, including details never published. He stops thinking of the ghost as a haunting and starts thinking of it as testimony. Beat: the theme crystallizes — memory itself is fighting back.

chapters.title: The Fire Drill Nobody Called
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Someone ransacks Tamsin's locker and torches his collected notes in a trash barrel; the fire alarm that should have sounded doesn't. Dee saw a board member's truck leaving. Beat: fear becomes personal; the stakes shift from history to Tamsin's safety.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Confession
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The librarian admits she was a secretary at the school in '98, ordered to purge Wren's records, and kept one program out of guilt. She gives him the key to the sealed record room above the gym. Beat: an adult ally, and the weight of thirty years of silence.

chapters.title: The Record Room
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Above the gym he finds boxes of sealed minutes: the board voted unanimously to classify the death as an accident, expel witnesses, and pay off the family. Wren's mother took the money and moved away; Wren herself had been expelled posthumously from the record entirely. Beat: cold fury.

chapters.title: Caught
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Pruitt catches them leaving the record room. He doesn't threaten — he offers: a glowing college recommendation, the lead in the musical, if Tamsin returns what he took and remembers nothing. Beat: corruption wearing its kindest face; Tamsin says yes and hates himself.

chapters.title: The Deal I Didn't Keep
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin pretends to accept while photocopying everything through Mrs. Okonkwo. The ghost's notes grow urgent, fragmentary — Wren's memory fraying as demolition nears. He realizes the notes will stop when the building falls. Beat: racing the clock; guilt sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for a Riot
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. With three weeks to opening night, Tamsin and Dee plan to embed Wren's testimony into the musical itself — projected pages, spoken names, the whole town in the audience. Allies trickle in: stage crew kids, a reporter ex-classmate, even Vey by phone. Beat: hope as an act of defiance.

chapters.title: Pruitt Cuts the Program
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The board cancels the musical outright, citing budget. The demolition date moves up — to opening weekend. Tamsin, cornered, makes the choice the whole book has bent toward: they'll perform anyway, uninvited, in the auditorium the night before the wrecking ball. Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: Opening Night
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Nine hundred people come — curiosity, loyalty, outrage. Mid-performance, the projections bloom: the minutes, the vote, Wren's name restored letter by letter in impossible ink across the curtain. The ghost is visible at last, standing in the wings where she died. Beat: triumphant, trembling catharsis.

chapters.title: What the Town Saw
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Fallout: the state attorney general opens an investigation; Pruitt resigns mid-scandal; the demolition is stayed pending review. Some townspeople thank Tamsin; others spit. Wren's elderly mother arrives, holding the one photo she saved. Beat: justice arriving imperfectly, outside the law that failed.

chapters.title: Letting Go of Wren
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In the emptying auditorium, Tamsin speaks aloud to Wren — tells her she was seen, that her name is on the marquee. The last note appears: 'Thank you. Now be loud for yourself.' The ink fades to ordinary black. Beat: grief and release; the haunting ends because the remembering began.

chapters.title: Graduation Day
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Commencement on the courthouse lawn: Tamsin speaks Wren Calloway's name from the podium and the crowd, this time, repeats it. A plaque is promised; a scholarship bears her name. Tamsin leaves for college not escaping but carrying the town's true story with him. Beat: earned, unsentimental hope.
